**Reduction.** A polynomial $P$ with coefficients in $[-7,7]$ (degree $\le 7$) is nearly tricky exactly when $P(4)=R(4)$ for some $R$ with coefficients in $\{-1,0,1\}$. Indeed, if $P=Q+R$ with $Q(4)=0$, then $P(4)=R(4)$. Conversely, if $P(4)=R(4)$, then $Q=P-R$ has integer coefficients and root 4.

**The set of values.** Let $S=\{R(4)\}$. Since $|d_i|\le 2$ and $4^i$ grows, the base-4 representation with digits in $\{-1,0,1\}$ is unique, so $|S|=3^8=6561$. These values satisfy $|v|\le 21845$.

**Counting.** $N=\sum_{v\in S} c(v)$, where $c(v)$ is the number of $P$ with coefficients in $[-7,7]$ and $P(4)=v$.

Write $P(4)=p_7\cdot 4^7+Y$, where $Y=\sum_{i<7}p_i4^i$ has $15^7$ coefficient choices. Then $c(v)=\sum_{k=-7}^{7} N_{\text{low}}(v-16384k)$, where $N_{\text{low}}(y)$ counts the lower-digit choices giving $Y=y$.

Since $N_{\text{low}}$ is smooth on the scale of the spacing $16384$, the sum over $k$ is essentially a Riemann sum, giving $c(v)\approx 15^7/16384\approx 10429$ for $|v|$ small. A Poisson-summation correction from the lower digits changes this by about $-0.25\%$ on average over $S$. So $c(v)\approx 10{,}400$ on average over $S$.

(A Gaussian approximation for the whole sum would be wrong here, because the top digit is uniform on 15 values rather than Gaussian.)

**Result.**
$$N \approx 6561 \times 10{,}404 \approx 6.83\times 10^{7}.$$

As a sanity check, this is about 2.7% of all $15^8\approx 2.56\times 10^9$ polynomials, which is consistent with 6561 reachable values spread over an effective range of about 245,000.

ANSWER: 68260000
